headline: Canarsie Pier by kayak: fluke in the deep holes, snappers everywhere else
subhead: With the flats baking under August sun, the bite has moved into the channels — and the bay's back-bay bluefish are building right on schedule.
body_markdown:
I took the kayak out of Canarsie Pier again this week instead of running the boat, and it wasn't about saving gas — it's about where the fish actually are right now. Mid-August, the flats in this bay turn into a bathtub by ten in the morning. If you want fluke, you need to get into the deeper holes and channels where there's still some current moving and the water hasn't cooked all day, and a kayak lets me slide into spots along the edges of Duck Point Marsh and the channel drop-offs near Ruffle Bar that a boat can't sit on comfortably without swinging on the anchor all day.

That's exactly where the fluke have been. Nothing spectacular — this isn't a five-fish limit kind of week — but if you work the deeper bends where the channel drops from six feet down to twelve or fourteen, on the last two hours of the outgoing, you can put together a couple of keepers. I've been dragging a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a half-ounce bucktail, bounced slow right on the bottom, and mixing in a strip of squid on the hook for scent. The takes have been soft — typical late-summer fluke behavior, lazy and picking rather than smashing — so I've been giving a beat before I set. Bay Streets and Head of Bay have both given up fish in that twelve-inch-to-just-shy-of-keeper range, with the occasional legal mixed in on the bigger drops.

The real story in the bay this week, though, is the bluefish, and I'm not going to pretend I didn't see this coming. We flagged it last week — said the snapper blues thick in the shallows were a sign the bigger class fish would keep building through late August — and that's exactly what's happening. If you've got kids or you just want steady, stupid-easy action, Canarsie Pier and the docks along Bergen Basin are lousy with snappers right now, one-inch to three-inch, hammering tiny silver spoons and bits of spearing under a bobber. But mixed in with them, especially in the last hour of light, I'm starting to see a few three- and four-pound blues showing up on light tackle — the kind of push that tells you the adult class fish are starting to filter in behind the peanut schools that have been building in the back creeks all month.

Striped bass are still around, but you have to work the tide right. Marine Parkway Bridge remains the most reliable spot in the whole zone, and it's still staging fish on the outgoing exactly like it always does — the current rips through those pilings and stacks bait against the structure, and bass sit in the eddies waiting for it to come to them. I fished the bridge on a Tuesday evening outgoing and picked up two schoolies and one just-shy-of-slot fish on a 3/4-ounce bucktail with a white curly tail trailer, worked with a slow lift-and-drop right along the shadow line of the pilings. Bunker schools have kept moving through the bay on this tide cycle, which is the same thing we called last week, and as long as that bait keeps pushing through the inlet, the bass will keep using the bridge as a feeding station on the ebb. It's not a blitz — you're working for two or three fish a trip right now — but it's consistent enough to plan an evening around.

Weakfish are scattered, which is about what I expected for mid-August. I've heard of a few being picked up on the channel edges off Cross Bay Bridge on the last of the incoming, working bucktails tipped with a sliver of squid down near bottom in eight to ten feet. It's not a target-species kind of bite yet — more of a bonus if you're already fluke fishing that stretch — but worth a few casts if you're in the neighborhood.

Out at Breezy Point and along Rockaway Beach, the surf has been quiet for stripers in daylight, which tracks with what's happening up and down this whole stretch of coast — warm water is pushing the bass bite into narrow windows right around dawn and dusk. If you want a shot at a beach bass right now, first light at Breezy with a swimming plug or a bucktail worked through the wash is still your best bet, but don't expect a long window. Porgies have been a nice consolation prize on the jetty rocks around the inlet — bloodworms or clam on a hi-lo rig in fifteen to twenty feet has been steady enough to keep a rod bent while you wait for something bigger.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change through the weekend. The tide cycle is easing toward the weaker phase before it rebuilds into the end-of-month full moon, so if anything, expect the bridge bite and the fluke pattern in the channels to hold steady rather than intensify. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd take the kayak back into the deeper holes on an outgoing morning tide before the sun gets high, then swing by Marine Parkway for the evening push. That combination has been paying off, and there's no reason to think it stops before Labor Day.
